senses: subject to someone, under one's authority
susceptible to danger, misfortune, or weakness, vulnerable
liable or addicted to a fault or failing, guilty of it
being security for a bond, debt, credit, etc., liable to be distressed, seized; extended to the debtor: answerable, e.g., by confinement or corporal punishment
la:adj:obnoxius.html:
ob-noxĭus, a, um, adj.
Lit.
Subject, liable to punishment, obnoxious to punishment, punishable: obnoxius poenae obligatus ob delictum, Paul. ex Müll.: ego tibi me obnoxium esse fateor culpae compotem,; : ego lege Aquiliā obnoxius sum,.—
Liable or addicted to a fault or failing, guilty of it (cf.: deditus, addictus); constr.
With dat.: animus neque delicto neque lubidini obnoxius,not addicted to vice or to sensual pleasures,: communi culpae,: facto,.—
With gen.: obnoxios criminum, digno supplicio subjectos, sepulturae tradi non vetamus,for, on account of,.—
Transf., in gen.
Subject, submissive, obedient, complying: dum illos obnoxios fidosque sibi faceret,: obnoxium atque subjectum esse alicui,; ; ; 37, 53, 4; 42, 46, 3; . —
Obliged, under obligation, beholden, indebted, responsible, answerable: uxori obnoxius sum,: totam Graeciam beneficio libertatis obnoxiam Romanis esse,: fratris radiis obnoxia Luna,: facies nullis obnoxia gemmis,not indebted to any jewels,: tantum in eo obnoxius est, si quid ipse dolo fecerit,.—
Exposed to a person, humbled before one: ne obnoxius filio sim et servo,.—
Submissive, abject, servile, slavish, mean-spirited, timid, cowardly, etc.: non quibus ego essem obnoxius,: summissaeque manus, faciesque obnoxia mansit,: si aut superbus, aut obnoxius videar,: pax,servile, dishonorable,.—
Subject, liable, exposed, obnoxious to any thing; with dat., ad, or in and acc.
With dat.: infidis consiliis obnoxius,: insidiis,: infelici fecunditate fortunae,exposed,: aemulationi, odio, privatis affectionibus,: morbo,: contumeliis,: bello,: plerique Crasso ex negotiis privatis obnoxii,: urbs artis itineribus (sc. incendiis),.—
With ad: terra solida ad tales casus obnoxia, exposed to such accidents (viz. earthquakes), .—
With in and acc.: in omnia obnoxius,exposed to every thing,. —
In gen., exposed or liable to injury, danger, or misfortune, weak, infirm, frail: in hoc obnoxio domicilio animus liber habitat,: supplex et obnoxius,: corpora,sickly, weakly,: flos,which soon falls off, soon suffers injury, frail, delicate,.—
Obnoxium est, it is hazardous, dangerous, .—Comp.: obnoxior (al. noxior),.—Hence, adv.: obnoxĭē (only in Plaut. and Liv.).
Guiltily, culpably: nihil obnoxie perire,quite innocently,.—
Submissively, slavishly, timidly: sententias dicere,.

la:verb:obnitor.gloss: to bear, press, push, struggle, or strive against
senses: to bear, press, push, struggle, or strive against
la:verb:obnitor.html:
ob-nītor, xus (rarely nīsus), 3 (
inf. obnitier for obniti, ), v. dep., to bear, press, push, struggle, or strive against any thing (mostly poet. and in post-Aug. prose; not in Cic. or Cæs.); constr. with the dat., acc., or absol.
Lit.: taurus Arboris obnixus trunco,: contra,: toto corpore obnitendum,: remi Obnixi crepuere,: densis ales (Lachm. aquila hinc) pinnis obnixa volabat Vento, Enn. ap. Prob. Lion. (Ann. v. 148 Vahl.): obnixi (al. obnisi) urgebant,.—In pass. signif.: obnixo genu scuto, set or pressed against, .— Of things: navigia fractas obnitier undas,.—
Trop.
To strive against, to resist, oppose (class. only in Part.): stant obnisi,: cum saepe obnitens repugnasset,; : stant obnixa omnia contra,: venti obnixi lacerant nubila,: adversis,.—
To strive, endeavor; with inf.: triumphum Pauli impedire obnitebantur,.—Hence, obnixus (obnīsus), a, um, P. a., steadfast, firm, resolute: (velim) obnixos vos stabili gradu impetum hostium excipere,: firmitas,: obnixus curam sub corde premebat,.—In neutr., adverb., resolutely, obstinately: obnixum. Pauline, taces,.—Hence, adv.: obnixē (obnīsē), lit., striving against; hence, in gen., with all one's strength, with might and main, strenuously, obstinately: obnixe omnia Facere,: oboedire, (dub.; Weissenb. enixe): petere, (Haase, enixe; v. Krebs, Antibarb. p. 781). —Comp.: argumentari,.

la:verb:obnuntio.html:
ob-nuntio (-nuncio), āvi, ātum, 1, v. a.
To tell, report, announce any thing bad or unfortunate: primus rescisco omnia: Primus porro obnuntio,.—
In augury, t. t., to announce an opposing, adverse, or evil omen (used both of the augurs and of the magistrates and tribunes of the people; cf. Smith's Antiq.): proprie obnuntiare dicuntur augures, qui aliquid mali ominis scaevumque viderint, Don. : augur auguri, consul consuli obnuntiāsti,: fretus sanctitate tribunatūs obnuntiavit consuli, etc.,.—Impers. pass.: ut sibi postero die in foro obnuntiaretur,.
